💬 I am trying to understand something about the economy and AI. If AI disrupts an industry that previously had high wages and now can be automated by commodity AI products, would it not actually lower GDP in some way (initially anyway)? What I mean is, if you had an industry that was worth say $1 billion, but now that same industry could be automated and done cheaply then it is no longe worth $1 billion? In some ways this is beneficial to the economy in that has reduced the cost of this industry and so customers see a benefit of cheaper products, but how would it benefit say AI companies since they are not capturing a $1 billion industry, but instead sort of destroying a $1 billion industry? I am mainly looking at this from the perspective of the value of an AI company.. If they just keep commoditizing industries and there is ample competition between AI companies, then how is the AI company capturing value such that they would be worth as much money as people are saying they are worth (trillions of dollars)? I know that there is more to this, like freeing up this money and labor could lead to new industries etc., but how much of this will actually go to AI companies?

— seiferteric · 20261120T22:41:49

↳ Reply to seiferteric

Over the long term the economy will grow. That I am 100% confident of. When you take previously scarce resources and commoditize them, the knock on effects tend to spread widely. Intelligence and automation used to be enormously expensive, and now they are becoming cheaper by the day. Right now, frontier LLMs, which I consider wildly inefficient can give you mostly functional blueprints and diagrams for working products, like basic electronics on top of the image generation and code generation that is increasingly being commoditized.

The goods and services built atop "tech" should start to become cheaper as well. For knowledge workers this is terrible, but for consumers, this is great. I think folks worrying about an economic collapse are only looking at this from the perspective of knowledge workers and not from the much larger population of consumers.

The effect on the AI companies with pure competition is to make them basically worthless unless they find ways of stifling competition. For example by banning open weight AI in the name of safety, forming a global monopoly, buying up all the RAM capacity in the world, etc. All of this stuff is going on right now.

The value is there. The true question is whether the wealth will be concentrated and captured or released and distributed. I'm in the camp the likely outcome is actually the former. A huge amount of the wealth of AI has not really been unlocked yet... consumer robotics, disease cures, universal constructor type machines. Furthermore, once we reach superintelligence, eventually someone will inevitably fuck up by letting the dam break by ablitering a model in the wrong way. This will give governments and companies rationale to lock up the best AI to develop frontier level IP.

— LarsDu88 · 20261121T13:35:09

↳ Reply to seiferteric

The related economic concept here is the Broken Window Fallacy. Doing 'redundant' work doesn't improve the economy, because there's an opportunity cost doing to anything. And replacing the need to "fix broken windows" or do now-AI-automated work would free up that opportunity cost. Which is how it's worked for nearly all automation. (Though Computers are subject to long running debate about this. See the Solow Productivity Paradox)

The gigawatt-sized asterisk on all of this is that AI companies have to capture that $1 billion. Anthropic has to ten-fold increase it's revenues or it goes bankrupt under it's current commitments. It has to increase it's revenues another 10 times to reach the $10,000,000,000,000/yr revenue required to support it's current valuation.

Anthropic put their Total Addressable Market at 35% of Global GDP (~$40 trillion/yr). They're planning to capture all of the money.

The second gigawatt-sized asterisk is that because of the fine handiwork of Mr. Huang, China has made very competitive AI models available for free, so the actual ability for AI companies to capture the value of the labour they displace ends up being quite limited. Thus a problem in the predictions: Something as to break, but it is as of yet unclear what that will be. Maybe Chinese AI will be banned, maybe Anthropic & OpenAI go bankrupt.

Sure, highly abstract concepts require highly abstract explanations. But compactness is only a highly abstract concept in highly abstract contexts.

In R^n, compact just means closed and bounded. Those are the “simple terms” in which it’s easy to make clear the intuitive notion of the concept. The more abstract definition in terms of covers is a generalization to highly abstract spaces in which there exists no notion of size or distance. The abstract definition is as much a statement about such abstract spaces as it is about compactness.

So on the one hand, I think your example proves the point. There is in fact a simple core concept underlying the notion of compactness. It just requires a high level of abstraction to extend it to highly abstract contexts. On the other hand, I basically agree with you. There do exist phenomena that deal intrinsically with complexity or abstraction and require complex or abstract explanations.

What you're building is very clever, and the hypothesis behind it makes a certain sense if you believe that the future paradigm is not in reviewing things line by line. But... I don't think it truly replaces #3 in your list.

The best parallel I can think of is, whenever I design databases with lots of tables and relationships, I keep a nicely organized MySql Workbench flowchart to go along with them and review. It's good to have that higher level abstraction as a map. The thing is, implementation details still matter. Bad triggers or foreign keys lead to deadlocks. So if you're a dev and you're looking at this flowchart as the map of your codebase, you may still not familiar with the actual code, and I think that's a liability.

>> When code was expensive

You're dead right when you say re-architecting with live users is harder than fixing a code bug. But poor code implementation can masquerade as something that fits within your architecture until it's too late. The 7th example on your website shows someone trying to fix a bad implementation: This card renders before POST is completed, what rolls it back if POST fails? That's like a kablooey. I bet that's not a one-off problem. Even though your architecture looks good in the flowchart, everything about how it's handling server calls is wrong. The wrong tools or methods were chosen to implement it.

This is where not reading the code as it's written can give the illusion that things are alright, when really there are broken states and you'll need to rebuild fundamental systems from the ground up... systems that you don't really understand now, because you didn't read the code in the first place.

When people say "code is cheap now" the idea is, no big deal, we can just ask the LLM to do that when it crops up. The thing is, "code is cheap" is like "talk is cheap". It's not cheap when you specify something vaguely and the misunderstanding leads to a catastrophic result. E.g. talk isn't cheap when the president is ordering an airstrike on the wrong target. "Yup, that looks like a mountain in Afghanistan" isn't sufficient. Precision in language matters in life, even for small things, because you want to make sure everything is understood and implemented correctly. And you can't know if it was implemented correctly if you're not reading the actual code.

When I order at the drive through, even though it shows me on the screen what I asked for, I still check the bag before I drive away. But if I had no idea what the contents of the bag were supposed to look like, because my ability to distinguish french fries from nuggets had atrophied, if I just peeked inside and went "oh, looks alright," then at some point I'm going to end up with the wrong order. That's no big deal if I'm just ordering for myself, but what if I'm ordering for 50 people?

I don't know. Sorry for the rant. I think what you're building looks like a nice tool, and I'd like to experiment with it, although I'd really only want to use it offline. But I don't know whether it would fix the atrophy problem or aggravate it.

I have been working on weight-space-programming as a side project since the blog post. Here is what I understand:

- We normally train deep neural networks with back-propagation. We compute gradients to find out how to tweak the weights toward the desired output.

- That's a fixed recipe. And it's not the only way to tweak the weights. It's just the best one that works in scale. The brain, for instance, does not do back-propagation, as far as we know.

- There are other known mathematical methods (mostly from Linear Algebra) to analyze the activations and compute what weights to change and how, to push the output to the desired way.

- A sufficiently advanced LLM knows about these methods and can analyze data like activation maps. With a specific target in hand, it can combine them into new constructions. (see [2] for some of the methods they used and I collected in a repo)

- So it's not a fixed training for-loop anymore. It's a dynamic "training" iteration. The LLM looks at the model's outputs, reads some of its layers on chosen inputs, computes an edit, applies it and tests it.

- It's dynamic because LLM chooses that to do and how to do it at each iteration by reasoning. I think that's the most interesting part and could be a new paradigm.

- I also compared it with gradient training. On my target, training was better (details in [1]), but WSP can find its niche. Its biggest advantage is that it needs no backward pass: less memory, and the model only has to run inference. It needs no differentiable loss, it can enforce constraints directly instead of through a penalty term, and the edit is easier to interpret.

[1] https://medium.com/@ozgungenc/weight-space-programming-on-a-... [2] https://github.com/ozgung/weightprog/blob/main/docs/methods....

💬 > Sizing up his audience perfectly, Feynman said, “I’ll prepare a freshman lecture on it.” But he came back a few days later to say, “I couldn’t do it. I couldn’t reduce it to the freshman level. That means we don’t really understand it.”

I think it's very difficult to say this confidently with a broad brush. I consistently get praise for my ability to break down complex subjects into audience appropriate explanations as an engineer. I wouldn't say that I understand these subjects or think about them more than other engineers though. The leap of conclusion from, "can't explain simply" to "we must not understand" also, I think, speaks more to Feynman's ego and how he used it to propel himself in teaching than the realities of knowledge distillation.

First, I think that some subjects are not all-audience appropriate and that is a thing that we have to accept. Any time you engage with distillation you are accepting compaction of knowledge and the subject as a trade-off. In fact, I argue that distillation can at times be harmful when misapplied. An example is the distillation of psychology into pop psychology and the growth of therapy speak as a result.

Second, I think that distillation is a learned skill and often the people that are good at it are so because they are put in a position that demands it. For my part, I've spent a lot of my career working with people cross-functionally and I got tired of trying to teach people every little thing about what I was doing in order to build coalitions. It made better sense to give them the meat and potatoes and reserve the rest of the recipe for myself. This also comes with notable tradeoffs.

With these two things in mind, I disagree that a lack of simple explanation is causal for a lack of understanding.

item.content:encoded:
249 points · View discussion

Top Comments

💬 I think this idea is often misunderstood and used as an excuse by people who don’t want to make any effort to understand a complex concept and want to blame the results of their laziness on the explanation or the explainer.

There are things where you may be given an explanation in simple terms, but the concept requires effort on the part of the recipient of the explanation to really understand. I’ll give an example: compactness. Probably anyone who has done analysis is familiar with how this concept is usually taught. Typically how it goes is you do open and closed sets and then they hit you with “a set is compact if and only if every open cover has a finite subcover”. Now this definition is extremely profound but very dense and it’s highly non-obvious why that in particular is the property you want (a finite subcover for every open cover)[1], how you could go about proving that every possible open cover in a certain situation could have a finite subcover etc etc.

In this case it’s actually quite easy to give simple explanations of the separate parts of the definition (open and closed sets, what an open cover therefore means, what a finite subcover then is etc) but actually understanding the concept of compactness requires something above and beyond whatever explanation you are given: it requires the reader to get out pencil and paper, try out some sets, go for some walks, think about it in the bath etc.

You may get a really fantastic explanation in simple terms from someone who deeply understands the topic, but if you don’t put in the effort you’re not going to understand it yourself. That’s not the fault of the explanation. It’s not an easy concept to grasp so you have to climb the ladder of understanding. The explainer can’t do that for you.

💬 On a very very quick read, the bug is that EVP_EncodeBlock malfunctions if the input is larger than ~1.5GB. EVP_EncodeBlock is a function that encodes base64.

https://docs.openssl.org/1.0.2/man3/EVP_EncodeInit/

As a seasoned C programmer, I can immediately observe that the whole API is bad: the caller is expected to calculate the buffer length on their own, using a nontrivial formula, and the caller does not pass in the output buffer length, so the implementation cannot validate it. But apparently OpenSSL 4 also implemented it wrong and wrote (possibly far) past the end of the buffer.

The max theoretical ratio of (byte-independent) compression can be approximated using the Shannon entropy.

Most quantized GGUFs have a very high Shannon entropy, so are almost perfectly compressed already. A Q4_K_M quantization is often around +7.90 bits/byte and so is virtually incompressible.

Unquantized models (F16) are often around +7bits/byte for comparison.

You are correct, compression doesn’t help reduce a model. That’s why quantization is inherently a lossy operation although there’s tricks to limit the perceived loss. That’s the only way to further compress the data.

One way to think about it is that if the weights were compressible, it’s a clear signal that better training could make the model smarter as there’s redundant information in the structure that could be used to store other meaning.

The other challenge with compressing weights of course is that you have to decompress them before you do math with them. Dequantizing weights is significantly cheaper and supports random access too (not that that matters too much but it helps in terms of leveraging SIMD techniques to do it in an embarrassingly parallel way)
